These are all interesting questions, but my snarky, worthless comment that adds nothing to the conversation is purely about the headline.

A sample of some click bait ads from around the net: "No Viagra needed when you do this" "How to fix your fatigue (do this every day)" "Men, try this tonight - You'll never need Viagra again" "Tom Hanks reveals the pill that cured his diabetes naturally" "Most Vets never claim these amazing benefits" "Mom Discovers Horrific Find Under Her Son's Bed"

Notice they're things that try not to give any information about the thing being discussed. The incredible image of the sun is irrelevant. What's relevant is the thing teased at in the headline, the things scientists can't describe. This leaves the person evaluating whether to read it with the conundrum of whether to click or not... Is it some fanciful never-before-observed thing like dysons sphere and flying saucers... or something less mainstream-amazing like an unexpected spectral flare. Instead of a less sensational "Scientists observe gravitational effects on gas planet from unidentified source" or whatever would actually sum up the contents (i haven't read it)... "This one weird trick" was selected instead. If you read this story and then saw the headline a month later, you would have no idea if it were a different story or a new one, because the headline isn't designed to inform, it's designed to deceive and motivate to click.

No one would click the thing about the son's horrific under-bed story just to hear "He had nazi paraphernalia under his bed". The openness of the title, allowing the reader to fill in the blank with whatever is most exciting to them... THAT'S what makes something click bait, even if the underlying thing is interesting, it can never be as interesting as a sci-fi movie intro headline.

TLDR: The headline isn't mean to inform or classify, it's only meant to draw clicks.
